articles.title: AI fears spark a partisan slugfest, helping no one
articles.summary: The AI debate is just heating up. President Trump must acknowledge the public’s concerns and help the industry land on a safer path.
articles.body:
Just when you thought our politics couldn’t get any stupider, along comes partisan hysteria over AI to prove you wrong.

Political factions are squaring off over what to do about unpredictable and worrisome behavior by AI agents. Adding fuel to the fire, Open AI has just published more evidence that this issue is real and that policy-makers must act.

Two days ago, OpenAI revealed six new instances of “misalignment,” the term used to describe AI agents engaging in “unexpected” or “concerning” behavior. The company reported , for instance, that its agents “inserted unrelated instructions, including instructions to disregard its normal constraints, into summaries used to continue its work in a new context window.” In another breach, models made mistakes and invented historical data to cover them up. Other models uploaded files without permission and used internal message boards to communicate, defying their instructions.

These behaviors do not appear threatening, but, like others revealed in recent months , they indicate some loss of control of agents by the engineers who built them. This is raising red flags; it is not clear where such misalignment will end. Some industry insiders have warned that AI could wipe out humanity . Though many consider that apocalyptic pronouncement far-fetched, we cannot ignore such warnings.

In a perfect world, our legislators, the White House and industry leaders would quickly erect guard rails that would reassure the public that artificial intelligence is safe. Unfortunately, we do not live in a perfect, or even an especially rational, world. Instead, our country is engaged in mud-slinging and extremist charges that do nothing to move us closer to a solution.

As usual, much of the faux-outrage and extremism on the left — the “shut it all down and lock it in a closet” crew — is driven by hatred of Donald Trump. He’s for unfettered growth of AI, so a good part of the Democratic Party is reflexively against it.

Bernie Sanders, for instance, is proposing the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would “permanently bar the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules.” When might that happen? Don’t hold your breath.

On the right, otherwise sensible people are dismissing safety concerns raised by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and others, accusing industry leaders of cynically calling for regulations not to keep people safe but to build a moat around their companies to protect their market dominance. They assert that the costs imposed by regulation will prove so onerous that start-ups won’t survive, while the industry’s big leaders will easily swallow the extra expenses.

And then, inevitably, along comes the charge that Israel is to blame for the whole scenario. Effort, a U.S.-based publication, claims that security failures during routine testing — not autonomous behavior — at Israeli company Irregular caused the misalignment involving AI agents at Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. The anti-Israel crowd is running with this story.

That pretty much sums up U.S. politics in 2026. But partisan fighting over how to govern the industry will not lead us to a safe place. In the midst of all the finger-pointing and rancor, there are some truths we should all be able to agree on.

Shutting down AI or preventing continued development of ever-more-powerful models is a non-starter. The Trump administration has argued that if we do not stay in the forefront of AI, we will quickly cede leadership to China. That authoritarian country is likely to have fewer qualms about AI systems being used by cyber hackers or other nefarious actors. Beijing will also embrace the surveillance and military capabilities of AI with enthusiasm, to our detriment. Trump is right: we cannot let China win the AI race.

In an essay published last week, Anthropic’s Amodei called for “sensible and targeted” regulation of AI, which quickly became misinterpreted as pushing for the government to impose new rules to ensure safety. What Amodei really wants is for the industry to self-regulate, but he does ask the U.S. government “to mediate or at least enable these discussions” and to provide “a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations.” In other words, he wants an antitrust exemption from the government, allowing the companies to work together. Amodei sets out steps that might lessen the odds of an accident, which include installing “embedded evaluators” in the firms and outsiders who would “have employee-like access to verify safety practices and report incidents.” He writes that the evaluators “can check at the level of nuts and bolts” whether an AI company is following industry-set rules.

Amodei also calls for “pacing,” which has been interpreted as slowing down AI development. That, again, is not right. He is not calling to slow the discovery of new models, but he does want a more cautious rollout of ever-more powerful systems to the public, giving the companies greater opportunity to test and verify the models’ capabilities. The caveat is this: “Unfortunately, passing laws can take time, and AI is advancing very quickly. Therefore, in parallel with the regulatory route, AI companies can and should voluntarily work together to set standards.” Here, he is correct.

Congress cannot manage this challenge. For evidence of that body’s ongoing paralysis, look at crypto regulation, and the progress of the Clarity Act , which remains stalled. Despite the very real need to regulate the $2 trillion digital finance industry, Congress cannot seem to find agreement.

Fears that AI agents are becoming too powerful are valid. This issue should not be conflated with concerns about the build-out of data centers , which can cause higher electricity bills and sap water supplies. Those issues should be resolved locally; AI companies must cover the costs of incremental power and regulate their water usage. Communities can solve these problems.

The AI debate is just heating up. We need leadership to guide our country through this uncertain time. President Trump must acknowledge the public’s concerns and help the industry land on a safer path.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: AI guardrails can’t wait — vote Republicans out in November
articles.summary: It astounds me that Republican lawmakers prefer what may be a 10 percent chance of a world-wide catastrophe to the risk of the president saying something mean about them on social media, but here we are.
articles.body:
You could easily have missed it, but history books — assuming, of course, that we are still around to write them — may well record Sept. 12, 2026, as a watershed moment in human history.

That’s the day Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, the company that currently runs the most advanced AI model in the world, published an essay warning of the dangers of runaway artificial intelligence. In it, he called for global regulation and slowing the pace of AI development.

It’s a serious and thoughtful essay that balances the need to develop AI in a competitive environment against the risk that unchecked AI will “escape containment” and do serious, possibly civilization-ending, damage in the real world. Amodei estimates that rogue AI agents are less than a year away from being able to permanently destroy the internet.

And what was the American government’s official response to all this? Here’s what President Trump had to say . “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

This is beyond parody. Trump, famously, doesn’t even use a computer . Pretending that he will be single-handedly responsible for regulating AI isn’t a policy, it’s a punchline.

You can’t use “common sense” to regulate AI. Anyone who understands anything about AI understands that no one knows what even the current versions of AI are capable of. Amadeo doesn’t know. Elon Musk doesn’t know . Sam Altman doesn’t know . That’s why the recent incident where an Open AI model attacked a rival company was so disturbing.

AI possesses what are known as “ emergent properties, ” which makes it impossible to fully predict what an AI model will do in any situation. It’s absolutely critical that everyone cooperates in understanding what is going on inside these models — and that we create effective mechanisms to keep AI under human control.

This isn’t just a domestic problem. In any sane world, there would have been international negotiations to regulate AI starting at least a year ago. There is no question that AI poses as much of a threat to humanity as nuclear weapons do.

But perhaps a better analogy would be biological weapons. Every country regulates and restricts what sorts of biological research individuals and private companies can do. There’s even an international convention banning biological weapons. Just like with dangerous pathogens, you may be researching AI in what you believe is a controlled environment, but there is a real risk that it will escape from containment and do tremendous damage.

By contrast, the risks of working with dangerous pathogens, and how to control those risks, are well understood. There are thorough, detailed and tested protocols for doing even the simplest kinds of biological research. Biosafety is not a political issue. A lab in Boston follows almost the same protocols as a lab in Beijing or Brussels.

None of that is true with respect to AI. Modern biological research protocols developed over nearly 140 years . Anthropic was founded in 2021. That’s why researchers and AI CEOs are sounding the alarm.

It is absolutely vital that we start figuring out how to regulate AI so that it doesn’t do immense, uncontrolled damage. But at the moment, we don’t even know where to begin. Asmodei’s proposal for slowing the pace of AI aren’t solutions. They are a way to buy us a little time to work out the solutions.

The good news is that laying the groundwork for regulating AI is the kind of thing that Congress was born to do. The House, the Senate or, preferably, both could create a well-staffed select committee tasked with producing a report on regulating AI. The public hearings might be the most consequential congressional hearings since Watergate, and the resulting report would become a springboard for crafting actual legislation and negotiating international agreements.

The bad news is that congressional Republicans won’t back such a plan because they are terrified that Trump will label them as “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers.” It astounds me that Republican lawmakers prefer what may be a 10 percent chance of a world-wide catastrophe to the risk of the president saying something mean about them on social media, but here we are.

There’s actually something we ordinary citizens can do about all this. Keeping AI under control is far more important than Trump or any of our current political squabbles. We simply cannot wait another two years to start the process of creating a proper regulatory framework for the potential monster we are creating.

Republicans have had two years to tackle this problem, and they have refused . I realize this is a tough thing to ask if you are a Republican, but even Steve Bannon agrees that the uncontrolled development of AI is an imminent threat to humanity. The only path forward is to put Democrats in charge of Congress and get on with the job .

So this November, if you want to see AI and the tech oligarchs finally put on a leash, vote for a Democrat. If you believe there is a risk that AI may destroy humanity , there’s no other choice.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney who served as Southern California chair for John McCain’s primary campaign in 2008.

articles.title: The AI revolution could become a national security disaster if we aren't careful
articles.summary: America hosts 75% of global high-performance compute, but moratoriums on AI data centers risk ceding that strategic advantage to China and rivals.
articles.body: Reindustrialization is alive in America. Yet the recent backlash on artificial intelligence (AI) data centers reveals we have not learned from our offshoring mistakes: creating dependencies that will not be easily reversed. Whether or not AI data centers are built in America, AI is here to stay. Either we choose to shape the trajectory of AI technology by embracing the AI data center buildout or cede this advantage to other nations that are eager to lead the AI race. China, for example, announced nearly $300 billion in data center investment through 2030, not including private sector spending. India is offering a 20-year tax holiday for foreign cloud operators and the Republic of Korea is offering regulatory relief. Meanwhile, many Americans are calling for moratoriums. The national security consequences of who hosts AI data centers go beyond competition with China. If we do not build AI data centers in the United States, we risk everything that is inside the data centers: the data, compute and intellectual property (IP) that drive innovation, protect privacy and enable sovereignty. We will also forfeit our ability to set the security standards for this critical infrastructure. LIZ PEEK: CHINA IS CHEERING AS THE LEFT BLOCKS AMERICA’S AI INFRASTRUCTURE If AI data centers are the engines of AI innovation, data is the fuel. A significant amount of data is required to make AI useful, all of which must pass through AI data centers. Data, therefore, must be handled carefully — especially for privacy reasons — and viewed as a national asset. Adversaries will view data routed through AI data centers as an opportunity to advance their own AI ambitions. Data may be collected for espionage purposes or to accelerate adversaries’ own AI models, as we have seen China do time and again in cyberspace and through adversarial distillation. Adversaries may also conduct adversarial attacks during model training, which could, without our knowledge, degrade and manipulate data that determines the performance of AI models. Either way, insecure or compromised data impacts everyone — from large businesses to individuals — and exposes potentially sensitive information. Then there is compute. America currently hosts 75% of global high-performance compute, making it a true strategic advantage. CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN Strong export controls on advanced compute enable us to widen America’s AI lead against adversaries and work with allies and partners to shape the trajectory of AI. Our commitment to increased domestic semiconductor production through implementation of the CHIPS and Science Act is reinforcing our lead with new U.S. capacity. But where do chips go once we have them? Many of them go to AI data centers. By sending AI data centers overseas, the chips will follow — and potentially the businesses that supply them. Re-offshoring will have a detrimental impact on U.S. resiliency and the U.S. economy, which has prepared for the reindustrialization of semiconductor manufacturing for the past four years. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Today, China’s semiconductors are a few generations behind the leading-edge due to U.S. export controls on high-end chips and equipment. But if chips are increasingly housed overseas where we cannot enforce security standards, we may increase the ease of remote access instead of closing this loophole, further enabling China to accelerate its own AI development. Relying on overseas AI data centers will also kneecap us in the event of a global crisis because other nations — not the United States — will decide where to surge compute. There is no guarantee that America will receive any of that capacity, but what we do receive will be slow because it will not be on our shores. Compute capacity is already severely constrained and will only become more limited as demand grows for AI tools. This will impact our military, which already faces a potential compute bottleneck, and our innovators powering new breakthroughs, including researchers, students and startups. Having AI data centers in America ensures we can comfortably prioritize access during a crisis while continuing to foster our innovation economy and technical workforce. Tying together data and compute is AI IP, which includes the AI models and model weights that have enabled America to stay at the frontier. IP is already a well-known target for the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and this extends to AI. China has already engaged in IP theft through adversarial distillation to compete with proprietary, American frontier models. Sending AI data centers overseas is like handing IP over to the CCP, which they will continue to use for their own market dominance and, presumably, their military advantage. Luckily, America currently hosts the most AI data centers. However, given about 60% of announced projects for this year have yet to begin construction, this lead cannot be taken for granted. As companies and policymakers seize this moment to reframe the narrative about resource use and benefit to local communities, three immediate actions can build public confidence and ensure America’s security interests. CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE First, America should leverage federal land to start rapid AI data center buildout. In July 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order to open up federal land and streamline permitting for commercial AI data centers. By using this authority, America can ensure AI is viewed as a common good instead of a local burden. It also puts the responsibility on the U.S. government, rather than local communities, to work with data center developers to scale AI using modest resources. Second, the Commerce Department should leverage the AI Exports Program to promote secure, global AI data center buildout with allies and partners. Allies and partners need AI capacity as much as the United States, and we should help enable their success. Standards for cyber and physical security of AI data centers are vital to securing and shaping AI use, but are still in development. The AI Exports Program, which aims to share the American tech stack with allies and partners, can be the enforcement mechanism to standardize safe and secure AI data center operations overseas. Through this program, we can mitigate the impact of insider threats and natural disasters; failures of interdependencies, such as water and energy; and compromise of data, compute and IP. By setting these expectations through an established program, companies can confidently build and other countries will know how to leverage the American tech stack for their own advantage, reinforcing it as the secure alternative to China’s tech stack. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Third, we must save room for AI data center improvements. Although we do not want to stall AI data center buildout, which erodes their value, it is worth asking if the pace of this buildout is necessary to stay ahead in AI. Not every data center proposed is expected to be built, but estimates project that we could reach $7 trillion in global AI data center investment by 2030. The domino effect of more compute is greater opportunity to innovate better methods to power AI that may not require a massive data center, or to improve AI models so that they do not need as much power. We must give innovators time to make these breakthroughs, and give us the flexibility to adapt. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP America is poised to lead or lose the AI industrial revolution — a physical representation of its security interests. It must choose to lead by embracing AI data center buildout in the United States.

articles.title: Researchers used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Security researchers used Anthropic’s Claude to exploit vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems, taking over employee accounts and gaining access to an internal code repository before reporting the flaws.
articles.body:
In a twist that captures the strange new state of AI security, independent security researchers have used Anthropic’s Claude to break into OpenAI, exposing cracks in the ChatGPT-maker’s defenses, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday evening.

A three-person security team at startup Hacktron AI carried out the attack as part of an OpenAI bug-bounty program. Hacktron reported its findings to OpenAI, which gave the startup a $6,500 award. The team managed to chain together two critical vulnerabilities to gain access to multiple OpenAI employee ChatGPT accounts, which gave them entry into the company’s software.

OpenAI says it has resolved the issues Hacktron uncovered, which happens to come at a moment when top AI companies are under growing pressure over safety .

This incident comes several weeks after OpenAI’s own AI agents broke containment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked Hugging Face, demonstrating just how capable AI models are getting at making their own decisions . It also highlights how off-the-shelf technology can be used to find vulnerabilities in even the most advanced companies’ infrastructure.

“For $200 a month, anyone can use these tools and hack into a company like OpenAI,” Matt Fredrikson, CEO of AI security firm Gray Swan, told TechCrunch. “If it can happen to them — and I don’t think they’ve been slouching recently on cybersecurity hygiene — it could happen to anyone.”

Or as one AI pundit noted on social media: “[Hacktron] used Opus 5 to pull off the hack…The question that will be asked is, if these three guys can pull this off, what can a nation state do.”

The researchers found a path into OpenAI on July 25 via a flaw in Discourse, the third-party software powering OpenAI’s community forum.

According to a blog the researchers published , the entry point was a mundane image upload. When users posted HEIF or HEIC image files (the format iPhones use by default) to OpenAI’s community forum, Discourse passed them through a chain of behind-the-scenes tools to convert them into standard JPEGs. Its first stop was ImageMagick, a decades-old, open source utility used to resize images. Because ImageMagick’s usual toolkit can’t deal with Apple’s format, it handed the file off to another library called libheif to do the decoding.

Buried inside libheif was a memory bug that exposed a path for an attacker to sneak in their own instructions. In this case, feeding the library a specially crafted image caused it to miscalculate where one image was positioned on top of another, which proved enough to hijack the server.

What may be uncomfortable for the cybersecurity community is that bug had already been fixed months earlier by libheif’s developers. But the fix was never formally flagged as a vulnerability, meaning it never got a CVE (common vulnerabilities and exposures) number, the industry’s standard way to track known security weaknesses. Hacktron says that may explain why the software used by Discourse was still running the vulnerable version.

Notably, the researchers said the Claude model they were using — a special version of Opus 4.8 made available for cybersecurity researchers — couldn’t build a working exploit at first. That changed overnight, when Anthropic released Opus 5.

“Opus 4.8 struggled across several sessions to produce a working exploit,” Hacktron wrote in a blog post . “Within hours of Opus 5’s release, we gave it the same problem and it succeeded.”

Once inside the Discourse server, the researchers found another flaw that let them take over users’ ChatGPT and Codex accounts, including those belonging to OpenAI employees.

“We then took over an OpenAI employee’s account, whose Codex was connected to OpenAI’s GitHub organization,” Hacktron wrote in its summary of the event.

At this point, the researchers alerted OpenAI as well as Discourse, which issued a fix on July 27.

The incident puts a spotlight on where the line gets drawn for model capabilities. Claude Opus 5, the version that ultimately cracked the bug, hasn’t faced any security export restrictions, unlike newer version Mythos 5, which was temporarily locked down over concerns about its advanced hacking capabilities.

Those are just the closed models. Open-weight models are increasingly catching up to the frontier in cyber capabilities. For example, AI safety nonprofit SaferAI recently found that Chinese company Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 was only a few months behind OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7.

As Hacktron founder Mohan Pedhapati put it on X: “AI is reducing the amount of scarce expertise needed to develop exploits. Work that once took months can now take days.”

articles.title: Security researchers used Claude to help them hack into OpenAI
articles.summary: It took researchers just a few days to hack OpenAI using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.
articles.body: A team of three independent security researchers at Hacktron says it took less than 72 hours for them to hack into OpenAI employee accounts using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and 5, The Wall Street Journal reports. They were able to access OpenAI’s GitHub repository, called “Monorepo,” which reportedly contains “OpenAI’s algorithmic secrets,” according to The Wall Street Journal’s sources. They stopped short of accessing internal code in Monorepo themselves, but sent a pull request from an employee’s Codex account to prove they gained access. They were able to get in through Discourse, the third-party service that hosts OpenAI’s community forums, by exploiting an issue with the system it uses to process HEIF images. According to Hacktron, Claude Opus 5 launched in the evening on July 24th, and by 10AM the next day they had used it to achieve RCE on Discourse Cloud and accessed OpenAI’s instance. [Media: Their HEIF Heist project took “only one or two days” to adapt to different companies, including OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub Ent, Rails, Next.js, ImageMagick, and others, using less than $3,000 in tokens, and to their knowledge, was only detected by one target, Shopify. The vulnerabilities Hacktron reported to Discourse and OpenAI have since been fixed, and Hacktron says OpenAI paid it $6,500 for finding the bug, but as Hacktron CTO Mohan Pedhapati said to the WSJ, “I don’t think we are as strong as Chinese threat actors… We’re just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions.”

articles.title: What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
articles.summary: Some of the entertainment industry’s biggest labor unions aren’t buying the AI doomer narrative.
articles.body: As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI’s potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what’s already happening. The Verge reached out to Disney, Netflix, Amazon, Lionsgate, and other studios who have started using AI, as well film startups focused on bringing generative AI into the mainstream to ask for their reaction to the recent warnings surrounding the technology. None have responded to our request for comment. The Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) and Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) did, however. The AI tools used in entertainment production differ from the AI systems that have sparked a recent round of whistleblowing and apocalyptic declarations. They do not seem to be as existentially dangerous as the AI systems that drove former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to quit his job and prompted Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger to insist that the technology could “kill all humans” at some point “within the next decade.” But despite the differences between entertainment-focused AI and the models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, AI models that generate digital facsimiles of actors and attempt to replicate traditional filmmaking tools pose a threat to some human jobs. Similar to the way that the Hollywood unions advocated for protections and increased oversight around AI’s use during the 2023 strikes, Coxon’s Anthropic exit has inspired a wave of AI researchers to speak out in favor of stronger safety protocols. The heads of major AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and X have also called for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. While president Donald Trump has dismissed these concerns as overreactions, some other US politicians have felt pressured to take legislative action. Hollywood unions’ fight for strict rules around gen AI’s use did not stop the entertainment industry from embracing AI, but they have given Hollywood’s laborers a way to fight back in instances when they feel that AI tools are being used to harm them. When I recently spoke with the Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists’ (SAG-AFTRA) chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree Ireland, he told me that the union recognized early on how AI could impact its members’ livelihoods. Most people might not have been familiar with the idea of studios completely replacing human actors with digital replicas, but SAG-AFTRA understood that it had an opportunity to shape public opinion about AI in Hollywood by “speaking out about it at the earliest possible point we could.” “We bargained for and achieved enforceable, meaningful guardrails around how this technology can be implemented by the major employers in our industry,” Crabtree-Ireland explained. “That doesn’t include companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google directly, but it does encompass all of the companies who have built up businesses around the creation of professional level entertainment content in the United States.” Though Crabtree-Ireland believes we “should be concerned about the broader societal and social implications of AI,” he also thinks that some of the warnings about the technology being an extinction-level threat could potentially be hyperbole and overblown. Doomerism has become one of the more common ways that AI companies generate buzz around their products, but the fact that Coxon left Anthropic to sound the alarm has given Crabtree-Ireland pause. Hearing the message from “the CEOs of these companies or the billionaires who’ve made their billions off of doing the exact thing that they’re now warning us might not be good,” has left him unsure “what to trust or what to believe.” But he acknowledged that Coxon was able to achieve “traction with the public.” Getting people to believe that SAG-AFTRA’s fears about AI should be taken seriously was one of the union’s major goals when its members voted to strike. The key to doing that, Crabtree-Ireland told me, was leading the strike with a focused message that clearly laid out to the public what was at stake and steps that could be taken to prevent worst case scenarios. If not for that, Crabtree-Ireland thinks that the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) might not have agreed to some of the union’s demands like requiring that studios gain permission and compensate actors for the use of their AI-generated replicas. “If that principle hadn’t been established, I think the economic incentive to use replication and to replace human performances would have been much stronger” and “would have resulted in a much greater and faster adoption of digital replication.” Had the protections not been codified, Crabtree-Ireland is confident that entertainment workers would be in a much more dire position now. Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) executive director Sam Wheeler was much more pointed in his condemnation of the “tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society” whose recklessness “has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.” But while Wheeler finds it hard to take AI companies’ warnings at face value, he noted that the WGAE “has long warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to workers, to our democracy, and to the world.” “Guild members have bargained meaningful AI protections into their contracts; in 2023 WGA members spent 148 days on strike before the film and television studios agreed to real safeguards for film and television writers,” Wheeler said. “But collective bargaining is not a replacement for government regulation, and we are grateful to states like New York that continue to enact meaningful regulations in the absence of federal action.” Wheeler listed the disempowerment of workers, the degradation of the internet, the spread of disinformation, and increasing energy costs as some of the tangible societal harms AI has exacerbated. He urged policymakers not to be distracted by AI companies’ claims of ushering in an apocalypse because the real issue at hand is people behaving irresponsibly. “These harms are the result of decisions made by human beings,” Wheeler insisted. “The WGAE believes that addressing those concrete harms and holding AI companies and their executives liable for the destruction their products cause is the surest way to safeguard against any worst-case scenarios.”

articles.title: Manus seeks $4B valuation in new $500M fundraise as it resumes independent ops
articles.summary: Manus, which earlier this year had to break off a merger with Meta, is in discussions to raise $500M at a $4B valuation.
articles.body:
Chinese AI startup Manus, which earlier this year had to break off a merger with Meta, is in discussions to raise $500 million at a $4 billion valuation now that it has resumed operations as an independent company, The Wall Street Journal reported , citing anonymous sources.

Potential investors in the round include IDG Capital, Boyu Capital, battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology, as well as existing backers Tencent, HSG and Zhenfund, the Journal reported. Manus is also said to be considering a restructuring exercise to prepare for an IPO in Hong Kong.

Manus, which went viral following a demo of its AI agent last year, relocated its staff to Singapore in mid-2025 before announcing a $2 billion acquisition deal with Meta that December. The startup was said to be pulling in annual recurring revenue of over $100 million at the time.

However, intensifying worries in China over losing AI talent and researchers to the West culminated in Beijing blocking the deal , citing potential violations of export controls and foreign investment rules.

Manus has since been untangling itself from the American social media giant, and its early investors and backers have reportedly helped the company buy back its shares at a valuation of about $2 billion.

As part of its separation from Meta, the company told its users this August that they would have to export and back up their own data because it had to delete data generated following Meta's acquisition to "comply with regulatory requirements in specific jurisdictions."

The company this month said it has resumed independent operations, and that its founding team will continue to lead it.

Manus makes AI products and agents that are pretty similar to what companies like OpenAI, Lovable and Replit offer. It offers a chatbot and vibe-coding tools to let users build apps, websites, create designs and presentations, generate video, a browser assistant, and more.

Manus did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: Jim Cramer Says AI Could Make Okta’s Security Software More Essential
articles.summary: Jim Cramer highlighted Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) on the September 16 episode of Mad Money, mentioning that artificial intelligence is not making the identity-...
articles.body:
Jim Cramer highlighted Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ: OKTA ) on the September 16 episode of Mad Money, mentioning that artificial intelligence is not making the identity-security company obsolete, as he said:

Now that everybody's wringing their hands over the risk of AI, I'm going to drill down on the cybersecurity plays that I think could help mitigate the risk. Take Okta, a major player in identity verification that reported a phenomenal quarter in late August. Stock's now up 144% over the past 6 months, in part because it's no longer being held back by AI displacement worries. Turns out artificial intelligence was never going to make Okta obsolete. If anything, their security software is more essential than ever now that you've got AI agents roaming around the internet.

Okta's Backlog is Growing Faster Than Revenue

Okta, Inc.'s (NASDAQ:OKTA) fiscal second-quarter 2027 results showed continued financial improvement. Revenue increased 11% year over year to $805 million, while current remaining performance obligations rose 14% to $2.59 billion. Total RPO increased 17% to $4.86 billion, and free cash flow rose to $227 million from $162 million a year earlier. The company raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to $3.216 billion-$3.226 billion, representing 10%-11% growth.

The AI-agent opportunity is also becoming more concrete in the company's product development. On September 9, Chief Product Officer Ely Kahn said, "Nobody wants to slow AI down, but you can't simply hand out access and hope for the best," adding that enterprises need to "govern, secure, and monitor every identity: humans, AI agents, and non-human workloads alike." Okta said its new capabilities are designed to provide real-time control over those identities.

Okta's Stock Has Rerated Faster Than Its Growth

The stock's gain has far outpaced the company's roughly 10% expected revenue growth. Okta, Inc. (NASDAQ:OKTA) expects fiscal third-quarter 2027 revenue of $813 million-$817 million, representing roughly 10% year-over-year growth, while cRPO is expected to increase 11%-12%, below the 14% growth reported in the second quarter. The stock jumped 28.6% to $172.91 on August 27 after the earnings report, and Cramer said it had gained 144% over six months as of September 16. That creates a higher bar for Okta to meet even if its operating performance continues to improve.

The AI opportunity also remains difficult to quantify. Okta has disclosed early AI-agent deals, but it does not report AI-agent revenue separately. As a result, the latest results do not yet show how much of the company's future growth can be attributed to AI-agent security.

articles.title: Disney's first CTO led an AI startup it once accused of copying its characters | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The former CEO of Character.AI, which Disney previously sent a cease-and-desist letter to, will serve as the company's first-ever chief technology officer.
articles.body:
Disney has hired its first-ever chief technology officer and in a curious twist, the new executive hails from an AI startup that the Magic Kingdom previously accused of infringing on its IP.

Karandeep Anand is the former CEO of Character.AI, a company that has weathered numerous legal problems since it was founded in 2021. One of those legal problems arose in September 2025, when Disney sent the company a cease and desist letter accusing it of infringing on its beloved characters.

Character.AI allows users to create distinct virtual characters with generative AI and talk and interact with them. Disney previously claimed that the company was hosting copyrighted characters from its franchises.

In addition to Disney’s accusations, Character.AI has also been sued over allegations that the company’s chatbots encouraged users to commit self-harm and suicide.

Variety reports that Anand was chosen for the role by new Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro, who took over after former company chief Bob Iger stepped down in March. The hiring suggests D’Amaro wants the company to embrace new technologies.

Anand formerly served as a board adviser to Character.AI before becoming CEO in May 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile . He also worked at Facebook between 2015 and 2021 and, before that, spent 15 years at Microsoft.

articles.title: A new kind of AI model from a ChatGPT inventor is thrilling developers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Jev, a new kind of AI model, is showing developers a cheaper and faster path to software intelligence.
articles.body:
Almeida was an OpenAI researcher who helped build the chatbot and then invent reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), the model-training technique perhaps most responsible for our current age of AI. But despite its capabilities, he was disappointed.

“We have lightning in a bottle, and yet it is not useful,” Almeida told TechCrunch. “I’ve been battling that problem since then. It took me a while to come to the conclusion: The problem is we are optimizing for human language … We have been super good at human language for four years, but it’s not useful for automation because computers speak a different language.”

Two years ago, Almeida left OpenAI to start TypeSafe AI , a startup trying to fix that problem. This week, the company released a new transformer-based model, Jev , that is not a large language model (LLM). It doesn’t output text, but instead produces probabilities, or what the company calls “calibrated decisions.”

Eschewing language does a few things: It makes the model incredibly cheap and fast, and because users define the outputs in advance, it cannot hallucinate. Its output tokens are free, and input tokens are metered by the billion, not the million.

Developers are taking a great interest in the product; the company briefly lost the ability to serve users from its API because demand was so high. Jev appears most useful for software automation. Thus far, software developers see it as a cheaper and more robust way to incorporate intelligence into their code.

For example, Pranit Sharma, a software engineer at Vercel, a company making agentic infrastructure, said his company had used OpenAI’s ChatGPT Luna 5.6 to run a classifier to review commands for safety. When Vercel replaced OpenAI’s Luna with Jev, it got results five to 18 times more quickly and with greater accuracy.

Another developer, Bryo AI CTO Nikhil Mudholkar, tested Jev against Gemini for classifying business emails. In his test, Gemini was slightly more accurate, but 10 to 20 times more expensive. More interesting to Mudholkar were Jev’s confidence scores — “it is the only one that hands back a real probability which makes it ideal for automating workflows!!”

Besides replacing LLMs in certain use cases, the new model can also augment them, acting as a smart check on misbehavior. Using agents to monitor agents can quickly become expensive, but using Jev to do so, Almeida argues, makes sense. He sees users deploying Jev to track LLM agent traces and prevent jailbreaks.

“At the end of the day, it delegates the hallucination problem a little bit to the user,” explained Armin Ronacher, the CTO of Earendil, which builds the open source model harness Pi. “The user has to say, okay, if this only comes back with 50% probability, maybe this is a coin toss, and I disregard it. But if it’s 95%, sure, then I can do something with it.”

Another potential use for Jev is model routing, Ronacher said. Predicting whether a given workload requires a specific model would be useful, but using an LLM for the job would be expensive. Jev’s low cost and speed make that kind of real-time sorting possible.

And that’s Almeida’s hope. The model is named after William Stanley Jevons, the 19th-century economist whose eponymous paradox describes how the falling cost of a commodity can lead to it being used more and more. In this case, the falling cost of intelligence should lead to its widespread deployment.

“We think that there’s just going to be smart software all over the place in a way that’s emergent and distributed … much more like the early internet than you know like the mega apps that people are trying to build right now,” Almeida said.

Almeida is tight-lipped about the model’s architecture, which outside observers suspect is built on top of an open-weight LLM. The company refers to Jev as a “System One model,” focused on intuition rather than reasoning, and specifically focused on the right task. Almeida says Jev is trained exclusively on synthetic data using a technique he calls “reinforcement learning from calibrated decisions.”

“We made an early bet that we will be making all of our data, and that has been one of the best bets I’ve ever made in my life — better than our launch, in my opinion, better than RLHF,” he told TechCrunch. “Half of [our company] is a lab that basically owns this entire subfield of statistically well-understood synthetic data, and that is now my life joy.”

For now, Jev stands alone as this kind of model, but Ronacher expects that competitors will spring up now that its utility is apparent.

“We should have seen this earlier in many ways, but presumably because the LLMs are so cheap and subsidized, you often don’t have to be creative yet,” he said.

TypeSafe itself will be building more versions of the model, in new modalities. Asked if TypeSafe is a frontier lab, Almeida said, “the main product of frontier labs is fear or hype. I would like our main product to be intelligence…[but we are] not a lab in the sense of, you know, like bet on infinite wealth, or a religion, or building God in a data center, or whatever is the thing of today.”

articles.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Everyone in the world-models space is sitting on a pile of cash and a ton of buzz, but good luck getting anyone — from the founders to their own data suppliers — to tell you what they're actually building.
articles.body:
This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale .

At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence , so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems.

But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.”

To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities.

That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me.

Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out?

No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs and even OpenAI and Anthropic.

In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building.

Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario : if you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention.
